newsitem.title: USA: Nigeria frees rates seeking international support.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria frees rates seeking international support.

text.p: Nigeria on Tuesday said it would free up interest rates to market forces, the latest in a series of reforms designed to win favour with the international community which all but shunned the country over its human rights record and economic mismanagement.
Finance Minister Anthony Ani told reporters he chose this week's annual meeting of the IMF and World Bank to make the announcement to "send the right signals to people here."
The meeting lures thousands of finance officials and bankers to Washington at a time when aid is dwindling and the world's emerging economies have to compete harder to attract private investors.

From Tuesday, the Nigerian government will remove the 21 percent ceiling on interest rates, which had the effect of propping up inefficient banks and keeping credit away from those who needed it most, Ani said.
At the same time, the government ended its system of allocating credits.
The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank have been pressing heavily-indebted Nigeria, which relies almost entirely on oil revenue to survive, to reform its economy.
Ani said he was also looking at ending the dual currency system where the official rate makes the naira four times more expensive than the market is prepared to pay.
"Nigeria's economy is very much on the mend. We are trying to control the economy much better," he said.
It was robust enough to ensure interest rates would not soar as they did last time the government tried to end the rate cap, central bank governor Paul Ogwuma said.
He predicted a continuing drop in inflation, while economic growth should be at least 6-7 percent next year, compared to no more than five percent this year.
Ani said Nigeria had to increasingly push for more private investment and intended to sell the government's majoirty stakes in oil joint-ventures and make revenues instead from taxes and royalties.
"There is no doubt in my mind that we have to privatise this sector," he said, adding management of the companies under the current system had led to problems and mistrust.
"If we are to grow we have to have more sectors where investors can come in," he added.
Earlier on Tuesday, the government appointed economic liberal Ernest Shonekan to head a committee of experts to plan for growth into the next century.
It also announced the creation of six new states as part of the transition to democracy and a return to civilian rule in two years.

At the weekend, the Commonwealth, which joins former members of the British Empire, decided not to impose sanctions and maintain a dialogue with Nigeria, which was suspended from the group after the executions last year of minority rights activists.
Ani said he also hopes that the international community will help Nigeria with its $32 billion-dollar debt burden, which eats up about a third of its annual export earnings.
"We should be eligible," he said of this week's agreement by industriasl countries to give some releif to the world's most heavily indebted developing countries.
About two-thirds of Nigeria's debt is owed to the so-called Paris Club of wealthy nation creditors which have agreed to write off up to 80 percent of a country's debts.
